implementation_notes: The classic realization is hand-written: keep `std::vector<Course> courses_;` private and publish `const_iterator` accessors (`std::vector<Course>::const_iterator begin()/end() const`) or a `const std::vector<Course>&` accessor, plus `add_course()`/`remove_course()` that mutate the container. `const` is C++'s protection proxy - a returned const reference or const iterator cannot be used to resize, erase or reorder the vector - which is exactly the capability Fowler attributes to const in C++. The classic form is still justified when callers need the container interface (size, algorithms, range-for) and the owner accepts that any mutation invalidates the view.
pitfalls: Returning `const std::vector<Course>&` looks safe but publishes the concrete container, and the reference is invalidated by any subsequent add/remove - storing it across calls is a dangling reference.
Const is not deep: `const std::vector<Course>&` still exposes non-const element access if Course hands out mutable members or pointers.
A non-const `begin()`/`end()` overload or a non-const accessor reopens membership mutation; keep the mutating overloads private or absent.

variants.name: std::span<const T> read view (C++20)
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 std::span publishes a non-owning pointer-and-length view of the private vector: `std::span<const Course> courses() const { return courses_; }` gives indexing, iteration, size and subviews with no allocation and no way to push or erase, because span has no mutating members. Pick it when reads are on a hot path or when only iteration/indexing is needed; keep the const-reference/iterator form below C++20 or when callers need the container interface itself (std::find on the vector, comparisons, capacity).
pitfalls: A span is non-owning: it must not outlive the vector, and every add/remove invalidates it (reallocation) - the caller cannot hold it across mutations.
std::span<const Course> protects membership, not elements: a const span over mutable Course objects still allows element mutation through const-correct accessors that return non-const references.
